1 Timothy — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Henry understands the purpose of this letter to be Paul instructing Timothy, whom he had left at Ephesus, in the selection of suitable church officers and the faithful administration of an orderly gospel ministry.

Paul also warned about false teachers, whose clever distinctions and endless disputes corrupted the gospel's purity and simplicity.

He urged Timothy to devote himself to this responsibility with diligence, faithfulness and zeal.

These themes occupy the first four chapters.

Chapter 5 gives directions concerning particular groups of people in the church.

The last chapter condemns quarrelling and contentious speculation, exposes the danger of loving money and calls wealthy people to good works.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe apostle salutes Timothy.1–4The design of the law as given by Moses.5–11Of his own conversion and call to the apostleship.12–17The obligation to maintain faith and a good conscience.18–20
Christ our hope; teaching that builds up faith (verses 1–4)

Jesus Christ is the Christian's hope.

Every hope we possess of everlasting life rests upon him.

When Christ lives within us, he is the hope of glory.

Paul appears to have been the one God used to bring Timothy to faith.

Timothy then served beside Paul in gospel ministry, like an obedient son working with a loving father.

Teaching that provokes endless uncertainty and argument does not build up the church.

Speculative disputes often tear down Christian fellowship rather than strengthen it.

The only way to preserve and grow in godliness of heart and conduct is to exercise faith continually in God's truth and promises through Jesus Christ.

The purpose of the law is genuine love (verses 5–11)

Anything that weakens our love for God or for fellow believers undermines the purpose of God's commandments.

The gospel fulfills its purpose when sinners, through repentance toward God and faith in Jesus Christ, are moved to practice Christian love.

People who are declared righteous in God's appointed way do not find the moral law an enemy.

But unless we are justified through faith in Christ and genuinely turn from sin, the law's curse still stands against us.

Even according to Christ's glorious gospel, an unrepentant person remains unfit for heaven's holy happiness.

Paul's conversion displays Christ's mercy to sinners (verses 12–17)

Paul knew he would justly have perished if the Lord had counted his sins strictly and judged him for every wrongdoing.

He survived spiritually only because of the extraordinary mercy and grace shown to him when he was dead in sin.

God worked faith and love for Jesus within his heart.

The statement is true and wholly reliable: the Son of God willingly and deliberately came into the world to save sinners.

No one who considers Paul's experience can reasonably doubt Christ's love or power to save someone who truly desires to trust him.

Jesus Christ died on the cross.

He now reigns on the throne of glory and saves all who come to God through him.

Let us praise the grace of God our Savior and give glory to Father, Son and Holy Spirit—three Persons in one Godhead—for everything accomplished in us, through us and for us.

Fight the good fight with faith and conscience (verses 18–20)

Christian ministry is warfare against sin and Satan under Jesus Christ, the Captain of salvation.

The good hopes other believers place in us ought to encourage us to perform our duty.

In every responsibility, we should seek an upright conscience.

Even the severest judgments of the early church were intended to stop further wrongdoing and bring the offender to repentance.

Anyone tempted to throw away a good conscience or use the gospel as an excuse for sin should remember that this is also the way to make shipwreck of faith.
classic_reading:
[1Tim.1.1-1Tim.1.4]
1 Timothy
The design of the epistle appears to be, that Timothy having been left at Ephesus, St. Paul wrote to instruct him in the choice of proper officers in the church, as well as in the exercise of a regular ministry. Also, to caution against the influence of false teachers, who by subtle distinctions and endless disputes, corrupted the purity and simplicity of the gospel. He presses upon him constant regard to the greatest diligence, faithfulness, and zeal. These subjects occupy the first four chapters; the fifth chapter instructs respecting particular classes; in the latter part, controversies and disputes are condemned, the love of money blamed, and the rich exhorted to good works.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The apostle salutes Timothy. | (1-4) |
The design of the law as given by Moses. | (5-11) |
Of his own conversion and call to the apostleship. | (12-17) |
The obligation to maintain faith and a good conscience. | (18-20) |
Verses 1-4
Jesus Christ is a Christian's hope; all our hopes of eternal life are built upon him; and Christ is in us the hope of glory. The apostle seems to have been the means of Timothy's conversion; who served with him in his ministry, as a dutiful son with a loving father. That which raises questions, is not for edifying; that which gives occasion for doubtful disputes, pulls down the church rather than builds it up. Godliness of heart and life can only be kept up and increased, by the exercise of faith in the truths and promises of God, through Jesus Christ.
[1Tim.1.5-1Tim.1.11]
Verses 5-11
Whatever tends to weaken love to God, or love to the brethren, tends to defeat the end of the commandment. The design of the gospel is answered, when sinners, through repentance towards God and faith in Jesus Christ, are brought to exercise Christian love. And as believers were righteous persons in God's appointed way, the law was not against them. But unless we are made righteous by faith in Christ, really repenting and forsaking sin, we are yet under the curse of the law, even according to the gospel of the blessed God, and are unfit to share the holy happiness of heaven.
[1Tim.1.12-1Tim.1.17]
Verses 12-17
The apostle knew that he would justly have perished, if the Lord had been extreme to mark what was amiss; and also if his grace and mercy had not been abundant to him when dead in sin, working faith and love to Christ in his heart. This is a faithful saying; these are true and faithful words, which may be depended on, That the Son of God came into the world, willingly and purposely to save sinners. No man, with Paul's example before him, can question the love and power of Christ to save him, if he really desires to trust in him as the Son of God, who once died on the cross, and now reigns upon the throne of glory, to save all that come to God through him. Let us then admire and praise the grace of God our Saviour; and ascribe to the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, three Persons in the unity of the Godhead, the glory of all done in, by, and for us.
[1Tim.1.18-1Tim.1.20]
Verses 18-20
The ministry is a warfare against sin and Satan; carried on under the Lord Jesus, who is the Captain of our salvation. The good hopes others have had of us, should stir us up to duty. And let us be upright in our conduct in all things. The design of the highest censures in the primitive church, was, to prevent further sin, and to reclaim the sinner. May all who are tempted to put away a good conscience, and to abuse the gospel, remember that this is the way to make shipwreck of faith also.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesPrayer to be made for all persons, since the grace of the gospel makes no difference of ranks or stations.1–7How men and women ought to behave, both in their religious and common life.8–15
Pray for everyone through Christ the one Mediator (verses 1–7)

Disciples of Jesus should be people who pray.

Christians should pray without excluding anyone on account of nation, religious group, social rank or party.

Our Christian responsibilities can be summed up in two words:

Godliness means worshiping God rightly.

Honesty means behaving well toward all people.

These obligations belong together.

Someone who refuses to give God what is due to him cannot be truly honest.

And someone dishonest toward neighbors cannot be truly godly.

We should abundantly practice what God our Savior regards as good and acceptable.

There is one Mediator, Jesus Christ, who gave himself as a ransom for all.

This saving way has been appointed for Jews and Gentiles from every nation.

Everyone willing to come by this way may approach God's mercy seat to seek forgiveness and reconciliation.

Sin created hostility between humanity and God.

Jesus Christ, our Mediator, establishes peace.

God appointed that his ransom and its blessings would become known at the proper time.

Before Christ came, the Old Testament spoke about his suffering and the glory that would follow, still awaiting their full revelation.

Those who are saved must come to knowledge of the truth, because God has appointed truth as the way of salvation.

We cannot be ruled by truth we do not know.

Prayer, modesty and the responsibilities of men and women (verses 8–15)

Under the gospel, prayer is not limited to a particular sacred building.

Believers should pray privately, with families, at meals, while traveling and in gathered worship, whether the meeting is large or small.

They must pray in love, without anger, hatred or hostility toward anyone.

They should pray with faith, rather than skepticism or contentious dispute.

Henry calls Christian women to modesty in clothing, avoiding pride in splendid, expensive or conspicuous appearance.

He says good works are the best adornment, precious in God's sight.

Cleanliness and a modest appearance should matter more than impressive fashion.

It would be good if professing Christians were free from vanity concerning clothes.

Instead of spending so much time and money adorning themselves and their children, they should give more to the sick and distressed.

Dress that contradicts a person's Christian profession or situation is not a harmless matter.

These are divine commands, not merely customs.

Henry follows Paul's restriction on women acting as public teachers in church, understanding that role as exercising authority.

He emphasizes, however, that believing women may and should teach their children the principles of true religion at home.

Women must also learn everything necessary for salvation.

Paul refers to the order of creation and to Eve's earlier participation in transgression.

But Henry also draws a word of comfort from the promise concerning childbearing.

He understands salvation “in” or “with” childbearing as coming through the Messiah born of a woman, with a word of comfort for those who continue in sobriety.

The particular suffering associated with childbearing should also move men to exercise authority with tenderness, gentleness and loving affection.
classic_reading:
[1Tim.2.1-1Tim.2.7]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
Prayer to be made for all persons, since the grace of the gospel makes no difference of ranks or stations. | (1-7) |
How men and women ought to behave, both in their religious and common life. | (8-15) |
Verses 1-7
The disciples of Christ must be praying people; all, without distinction of nation, sect, rank, or party. Our duty as Christians, is summed up in two words; godliness, that is, the right worshipping of God; and honesty, that is, good conduct toward all men. These must go together: we are not truly honest, if we are not godly, and do not render to God his due; and we are not truly godly, if not honest. What is acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour, we should abound in. There is one Mediator, and that Mediator gave himself a ransom for all. And this appointment has been made for the benefit of the Jews and the Gentiles of every nation; that all who are willing may come in this way, to the mercy-seat of a pardoning God, to seek reconciliation with him. Sin had made a quarrel between us and God; Jesus Christ is the Mediator who makes peace. He is a ransom that was to be known in due time. In the Old Testament times, his sufferings, and the glory that should follow, were spoken of as things to be revealed in the last times. Those who are saved must come to the knowledge of the truth, for that is God's appointed way to save sinners: if we do not know the truth, we cannot be ruled by it.
[1Tim.2.8-1Tim.2.15]
Verses 8-15
Under the gospel, prayer is not to be confined to any one particular house of prayer, but men must pray every where. We must pray in our closets, pray in our families, pray at our meals, pray when we are on journeys, and pray in the solemn assemblies, whether more public or private. We must pray in charity; without wrath, or malice, or anger at any person. We must pray in faith, without doubting, and without disputing. Women who profess the Christian religion, must be modest in apparel, not affecting gaudiness, gaiety, or costliness. Good works are the best ornament; these are, in the sight of God, of great price. Modesty and neatness are more to be consulted in garments than elegance and fashion. And it would be well if the professors of serious godliness were wholly free from vanity in dress. They should spend more time and money in relieving the sick and distressed, than in decorating themselves and their children. To do this in a manner unsuitable to their rank in life, and their profession of godliness, is sinful. These are not trifles, but Divine commands. The best ornaments for professors of godliness, are good works. According to St. Paul, women are not allowed to be public teachers in the church; for teaching is an office of authority. But good women may and ought to teach their children at home the principles of true religion. Also, women must not think themselves excused from learning what is necessary to salvation, though they must not usurp authority. As woman was last in the creation, which is one reason for her subjection, so she was first in the transgression. But there is a word of comfort; that those who continue in sobriety, shall be saved in child-bearing, or with child-bearing, by the Messiah, who was born of a woman. And the especial sorrow to which the female sex is subject, should cause men to exercise their authority with much gentleness, tenderness, and affection.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe qualifications and behaviour of gospel bishops.1–7And of deacons and their wives.8–13The reason of writing about these, and other church affairs.14–16
The character required of an overseer (verses 1–7)

When a man desires the pastoral office from genuine love for Jesus Christ and concern for human souls, and is willing to deny himself and endure hardship by devoting his life to that work, he desires a good work.

Such an ambition deserves approval if the person also possesses the required qualifications.

A minister should give others as little just reason for complaint as possible.

Otherwise his behavior may bring disgrace upon the office he holds.

He ought to be sober, self-controlled and moderate in his actions and in his enjoyment of the created comforts God provides.

Scripture connects sobriety and watchfulness because each supports the other.

The families of ministers should be good examples to other families.

Beware of pride!

Pride was the sin that turned angels into devils.

A minister should have a good reputation among neighbors, with no justified scandal arising from his past conduct.

To encourage ministers who serve faithfully, Christ has made this gracious promise:

“I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

He will equip his ministers for their duties, sustain them through difficulties, comfort them amid their work and reward their faithfulness.

The integrity required of deacons (verses 8–13)

Deacons were first appointed to distribute the church's charitable assistance and manage its affairs.

Henry notes that some among the early deacons also became pastors or evangelists.

Deacons therefore received an important public trust.

They must be serious, prudent and dependable.

We should not entrust a public responsibility to anyone until that person has demonstrated fitness for the work involved.

People closely associated with ministers also need to live in a way consistent with Christ's gospel.

The church proclaims the mystery of godliness (verses 14–16)

The church is God's household and dwelling place.

It upholds and displays Scripture and Christ's teaching, much like a pillar holding up a public proclamation.

When a church abandons its role as pillar and foundation of the truth, believers may and should leave it.

Loyalty to God's truth must come first.

The great mystery of godliness concerns Jesus Christ.

He is God who became human and appeared in human flesh.

God was pleased to reveal himself to the human race by his Son taking human nature.

Although Christ was accused of being a sinner and put to death as a criminal, he was raised by the Spirit, vindicated against every false charge.

Angels attended and served him, because he is their Lord.

The Gentiles welcomed the gospel that the Jews rejected.

Remember that God was revealed in the flesh to take away our sins, redeem us from all lawlessness and purify a people for himself eager to perform good works.

These magnificent teachings must be made visible through the Spirit's fruit in our conduct.
classic_reading:
[1Tim.3.1-1Tim.3.7]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The qualifications and behaviour of gospel bishops. | (1-7) |
And of deacons and their wives. | (8-13) |
The reason of writing about these, and other church affairs. | (14-16) |
Verses 1-7
If a man desired the pastoral office, and from love to Christ, and the souls of men, was ready to deny himself, and undergo hardships by devoting himself to that service, he sought to be employed in a good work, and his desire should be approved, provided he was qualified for the office. A minister must give as little occasion for blame as can be, lest he bring reproach upon his office. He must be sober, temperate, moderate in all his actions, and in the use of all creature-comforts. Sobriety and watchfulness are put together in Scripture, they assist one the other. The families of ministers ought to be examples of good to all other families. We should take heed of pride; it is a sin that turned angels into devils. He must be of good repute among his neighbours, and under no reproach from his former life. To encourage all faithful ministers, we have Christ's gracious word of promise, Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world, [Matt.28.20] Mt 28:20. And he will fit his ministers for their work, and carry them through difficulties with comfort, and reward their faithfulness.
[1Tim.3.8-1Tim.3.13]
Verses 8-13
The deacons were at first appointed to distribute the charity of the church, and to manage its concerns, yet pastors and evangelists were among them. The deacons had a great trust reposed in them. They must be grave, serious, prudent men. It is not fit that public trusts should be lodged in the hands of any, till they are found fit for the business with which they are to be trusted. All who are related to ministers, must take great care to walk as becomes the gospel of Christ.
[1Tim.3.14-1Tim.3.16]
Verses 14-16
The church is the house of God; he dwells there. The church holds forth the Scripture and the doctrine of Christ, as a pillar holds forth a proclamation. When a church ceases to be the pillar and ground of truth, we may and ought to forsake her; for our regard to truth should be first and greatest. The mystery of godliness is Christ. He is God, who was made flesh, and was manifest in the flesh. God was pleased to manifest himself to man, by his own Son taking the nature of man. Though reproached as a sinner, and put to death as a malefactor, Christ was raised again by the Spirit, and so was justified from all the false charges with which he was loaded. Angels ministered to him, for he is the Lord of angels. The Gentiles welcomed the gospel which the Jews rejected. Let us remember that God was manifest in the flesh, to take away our sins, to redeem us from all iniquity, and to purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works. These doctrines must be shown forth by the fruits of the Spirit in our lives.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesOf departures from the faith that began already to appear.1–5Several directions, with motives for due discharge of duties.6–16
Reject false restrictions and receive God's gifts with thanks (verses 1–5)

The Holy Spirit spoke in both the Old and New Testaments of a widespread departure from faith in Christ and the pure worship of God.

This would occur during the Christian era, described as the last days.

Some false teachers declare evil what God has permitted.

Others command as necessary duties what he has left to human freedom.

God has given us more than enough opportunity for watchfulness, self-denial and obedience through his actual commandments.

We do not need invented duties that forbid the things he has allowed.

Nevertheless, permission never justifies immoderate or improper use of God's gifts.

Nothing we receive will truly benefit us unless we seek his blessing upon it through prayer.

Godliness is more valuable than outward self-denial (verses 6–10)

External forms of restraint have only limited value.

What good is it to discipline the body while failing to put sin itself to death?

The hardest work performed merely in outward practices cannot make a person holy.

The great value of godliness rests partly upon God's promises.

Those promises include blessings in this present life, but especially in the life to come.

When we lose something for Christ's sake, we will not ultimately lose through belonging to Christ.

Christ is described as Savior of all people.

How much more will he reward those who sincerely seek him and serve him!

He will provide what is truly good for those whom he has made new creations.

Teach by doctrine and example, even when young (verses 11–16)

Young people's age will not make them contemptible if they avoid vanity, foolish behavior and corrupt habits.

Those who teach others through doctrine must also teach through their lives.

Their words should build up believers, and their conduct should be holy.

They should be examples of love for God and for faithful people, and of heavenly-mindedness.

Ministers ought to regard these responsibilities as their principal calling and work.

Through such diligence, their progress will become visible, benefiting both themselves and other people.

This is the path toward growing in knowledge and grace while helping others grow as well.

A minister's doctrine must be biblical, clear, centered on the gospel and practical.

It should be carefully stated, explained, defended and applied.

Such responsibilities leave little time for pursuing worldly pleasures, pointless social visits, frivolous conversation or purely decorative amusements.

May every believer also grow in a way that others can recognize.

May each seek to experience the gospel's power within the soul and produce its fruit in daily conduct.
classic_reading:
[1Tim.4.1-1Tim.4.5]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
Of departures from the faith that began already to appear. | (1-5) |
Several directions, with motives for due discharge of duties. | (6-16) |
Verses 1-5
The Holy Spirit, both in the Old and the New Testament, spoke of a general turning from the faith of Christ, and the pure worship of God. This should come during the Christian dispensation, for those are called the latter days. False teachers forbid as evil what God has allowed, and command as a duty what he has left indifferent. We find exercise for watchfulness and self-denial, in attending to the requirements of God's law, without being tasked to imaginary duties, which reject what he has allowed. But nothing justifies an intemperate or improper use of things; and nothing will be good to us, unless we seek by prayer for the Lord's blessing upon it.
[1Tim.4.6-1Tim.4.10]
Verses 6-10
Outward acts of self-denial profit little. What will it avail us to mortify the body, if we do not mortify sin? No diligence in mere outward things could be of much use. The gain of godliness lies much in the promise; and the promises to godly people relate partly to the life that now is, but especially to the life which is to come: though we lose for Christ, we shall not lose by him. If Christ be thus the Saviour of all men, then much more will he be the Rewarder of those who seek and serve him; he will provide well for those whom he has made new creatures.
[1Tim.4.11-1Tim.4.16]
Verses 11-16
Men's youth will not be despised, if they keep from vanities and follies. Those who teach by their doctrine, must teach by their life. Their discourse must be edifying; their conversation must be holy; they must be examples of love to God and all good men, examples of spiritual-mindedness. Ministers must mind these things as their principal work and business. By this means their profiting will appear in all things, as well as to all persons; this is the way to profit in knowledge and grace, and also to profit others. The doctrine of a minister of Christ must be scriptural, clear, evangelical, and practical; well stated, explained, defended, and applied. But these duties leave no leisure for wordly pleasures, trifling visits, or idle conversation, and but little for what is mere amusement, and only ornamental. May every believer be enabled to let his profiting appear unto all men; seeking to experience the power of the gospel in his own soul, and to bring forth its fruits in his life.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesDirections as to the elder and younger men and women.1, 2And as to poor widows.3–8Concerning widows.9–16The respect to be paid to elders. Timothy is to take care in rebuking offenders, in ordaining ministers, and as to his own health.17–25
Correct others with respect and gentleness (verses 1 and 2)

We should respect people according to their age and responsibilities.

When someone younger has acted wrongly, correction should never be given from a desire to find fault.

It should be motivated by a desire to help that person grow.

Great meekness, wisdom and care are required when correcting anyone, even when correction is clearly deserved.

Care for widows and needy family members (verses 3–8)

Honor widows who are truly without support.

Provide practical relief and assistance for their needs.

When parents become poor and their children possess the means to help, those children have a duty to support them as fully as they can.

Widowhood can bring deep loneliness and distress.

But widows should trust the Lord and continue in prayer.

Anyone who lives entirely for worldly pleasure is spiritually dead while still physically alive.

How many professing Christians live in that condition, even into old age!

Men and women who refuse to support needy relatives effectively deny the faith they profess.

If they spend on sinful indulgence what should have been used to maintain their households, their conduct is worse than that of unbelievers.

A professing Christian who embraces corrupt ideas or practices can bring greater dishonor upon the faith than someone who has never claimed to believe it.

Faithful charity and suitable church service (verses 9–16)

Anyone appointed to public church service must be free from justified accusations of wrongdoing.

Some people may be worthy recipients of charitable help without being suitable for an official ministry role.

Those wishing to receive mercy in adversity should be willing to show mercy in prosperity.

People who are eager to perform good work generally prove faithful when entrusted with responsibility.

Those who become idle rarely remain merely inactive.

They often begin interfering in the affairs of neighbors and sowing discord among fellow believers.

Christians should relieve destitute relatives whenever possible.

That allows the church to direct its shared resources toward those who are completely abandoned and have no relatives able to help them.

Honor faithful ministers and judge without favoritism (verses 17–25)

Churches must provide adequate material support for ministers.

Those who labor diligently in teaching and leading God's people deserve special honor and esteem.

That support is their rightful due, just as an employee deserves payment for work performed.

Paul solemnly instructed Timothy not to show favoritism.

We must continually guard against participating in other people's sins.

Keep yourself pure—not only by avoiding similar misconduct, but also by refusing to approve, encourage or assist wrongdoing by others.

Paul also instructed Timothy to care for his physical health.

We should neither make our bodies masters that control our lives nor treat them as slaves to be abused.

Instead, care for them so that they remain as useful as possible for serving God.

Some sins are visible to everyone long before judgment.

Others remain concealed for a time.

Yet the Lord will bring hidden acts and the true purposes of every heart into the light.

Remembering that day, let everyone fulfill their responsibilities—whether public or private, high or low—so that God's name and teaching are never disgraced through our conduct.
classic_reading:
[1Tim.5.1-1Tim.5.2]
Chapter 5
Chapter Outline
Directions as to the elder and younger men and women. | (1-2) |
And as to poor widows. | (3-8) |
Concerning widows. | (9-16) |
The respect to be paid to elders. Timothy is to take care in rebuking offenders, in ordaining ministers, and as to his own health. | (17-25) |
Verses 1-2
Respect must be paid to the dignity of years and place. The younger, if faulty, must be rebuked, not as desirous to find fault with them, but as willing to make the best of them. There is need of much meekness and care in reproving those who deserve reproof.
[1Tim.5.3-1Tim.5.8]
Verses 3-8
Honour widows that are widows indeed, relieve them, and maintain them. It is the duty of children, if their parents are in need, and they are able to relieve them, to do it to the utmost of their power. Widowhood is a desolate state; but let widows trust in the Lord, and continue in prayer. All who live in pleasure, are dead while they live, spiritually dead, dead in trespasses and sins. Alas, what numbers there are of this description among nominal Christians, even to the latest period of life! If any men or women do not maintain their poor relations, they in effect deny the faith. If they spend upon their lusts and pleasures, what should maintain their families, they have denied the faith, and are worse than infidels. If professors of the gospel give way to any corrupt principle or conduct, they are worse than those who do not profess to believe the doctrines of grace.
[1Tim.5.9-1Tim.5.16]
Verses 9-16
Every one brought into any office in the church, should be free from just censure; and many are proper objects of charity, yet ought not to be employed in public services. Those who would find mercy when they are in distress, must show mercy when they are in prosperity; and those who show most readiness for every good work, are most likely to be faithful in whatever is trusted to them. Those who are idle, very seldom are only idle, they make mischief among neighbours, and sow discord among brethren. All believers are required to relieve those belonging to their families who are destitute, that the church may not be prevented from relieving such as are entirely destitute and friendless.
[1Tim.5.17-1Tim.5.25]
Verses 17-25
Care must be taken that ministers are maintained. And those who are laborious in this work are worthy of double honour and esteem. It is their just due, as much as the reward of the labourer. The apostle charges Timothy solemnly to guard against partiality. We have great need to watch at all times, that we do not partake of other men's sins. Keep thyself pure, not only from doing the like thyself, but from countenancing it, or any way helping to it in others. The apostle also charges Timothy to take care of his health. As we are not to make our bodies masters, so neither slaves; but to use them so that they may be most helpful to us in the service of God. There are secret, and there are open sins: some men's sins are open before-hand, and going before unto judgment; some they follow after. God will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and make known the counsels of all hearts. Looking forward to the judgment-day, let us all attend to our proper offices, whether in higher or lower stations, studying that the name and doctrine of God may never be blasphemed on our account.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe duty of Christians towards believing, as well as other masters.1–5The advantage of godliness with contentment.6–10A solemn charge to Timothy to be faithful.11–16The apostle repeats his warning to the rich, and closes with a blessing.17–21
Respect lawful authority and reject teaching driven by greed (verses 1–5)

Christians should not imagine that greater religious knowledge or privilege gives them permission to despise unbelieving masters, disregard lawful duties or expose employers' faults maliciously.

Those whose masters also believe in Christ must not withhold proper respect merely because they share equal spiritual privileges.

Instead, their common faith should move them to serve with greater diligence and goodwill.

The only teaching to which we must give unconditional agreement is the sound teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ.

People who know very little are often the proudest, precisely because they do not know themselves well.

Pride leads to envy, quarrels, insults, hostile suspicions and useless disputes.

These arguments may sound clever but contain no solid spiritual truth.

They arise in minds corrupted by sinful desires, ignorant of the gospel's transforming power and motivated by worldly advantage.

Godliness joined with contentment is great gain (verses 6–10)

Those who turn Christianity into a business for their own worldly advancement will eventually be disappointed.

But those who make godliness their true calling can rely upon God's promises for this life and the life to come.

Genuine believers can know their final happiness is secure.

When they are also content with their present circumstances, they already have enough.

Even in the greatest poverty, we cannot own less than we possessed when we were born.

At death, even the richest person can finally carry away little more than a burial shroud, coffin and grave.

Nature can be satisfied with relatively little.

If our natural needs can be content with a little, grace should be content with even less.

The necessary things of life should limit the Christian's ambitions.

With food and clothing, we should seek to remain thankful.

Consider the danger of greed.

Paul does not condemn everyone who is rich.

He warns those who are determined to become rich—people who place their happiness in wealth and pursue it as their highest goal.

Such people expose themselves to the devil's temptations.

They may turn to dishonest methods to increase their possessions.

They may become so overwhelmed by business that they have no time or desire left for spiritual duties.

They may enter relationships that draw them into wrongdoing and folly.

What sin will love of money not draw people toward?

Someone may possess a great deal of money without loving it.

But where money is loved as an idol, it drives the person toward every kind of evil.

Different sins and vices grow out of this root in different ways.

We can see examples everywhere, especially in periods of wealth, luxury and careless religious profession.

Fight the good fight and live for eternal things (verses 11–16)

No one should set the heart upon earthly possessions, but such attachment is particularly inappropriate in a servant of God.

Those who belong to the Lord should concentrate upon his purposes and commands.

Christian life involves genuine conflict with corruption, temptation and the powers of darkness.

Eternal life is the crown offered to strengthen our determination.

We are called to take hold of it.

Those who possess much wealth especially need clear instruction about its dangers and proper uses.

But a minister cannot warn them sincerely while secretly craving the very pleasures their money can purchase.

Christ's return is certain.

Its exact time is not ours to know.

The radiance of God's glory is more than mortal eyes can bear.

We can approach him only as he has made himself known to sinners in and through Jesus Christ.

Henry explains that this passage adores the divine nature without distinguishing the Persons, because its statements are true of Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

God has made himself known to us through the human nature of Jesus, the Father's only-begotten Son.

Be rich in good works, not merely possessions (verses 17–21)

Being wealthy in this world is entirely different from being rich toward God.

Few things are more uncertain than earthly wealth.

Rich people should recognize that God is the One who gives wealth.

Only he can also give them the heart to enjoy it rightly.

Many people own much but obtain little true comfort from it because they cannot use it wisely or generously.

What good is a large estate except as an opportunity to do more good?

Let genuine faith in Christ show itself through loving actions and generosity.

Take hold of eternal life rather than following the self-indulgent, greedy and ungodly, who will eventually lift up their eyes in torment.

Knowledge that contradicts the truth of Christ's gospel is not genuine wisdom.

If it were true knowledge, it would recognize and welcome gospel truth.

People who elevate human speculation above faith risk abandoning the faith altogether.

Grace contains every spiritual good.

Grace is the beginning and pledge of glory.

Where God genuinely gives his grace, he will also bring the person into glory.
classic_reading:
[1Tim.6.1-1Tim.6.5]
Chapter 6
Chapter Outline
The duty of Christians towards believing, as well as other masters. | (1-5) |
The advantage of godliness with contentment. | (6-10) |
A solemn charge to Timothy to be faithful. | (11-16) |
The apostle repeats his warning to the rich, and closes with a blessing. | (17-21) |
Verses 1-5
Christians were not to suppose that religious knowledge, or Christian privileges, gave them any right to despise heathen masters, or to disobey lawful commands, or to expose their faults to others. And such as enjoyed the privilege of living with believing masters, were not to withhold due respect and reverence, because they were equal in respect to religious privileges, but were to serve with double diligence and cheerfulness, because of their faith in Christ, and as partakers of his free salvation. We are not to consent to any words as wholesome, except the words of our Lord Jesus Christ; to these we must give unfeigned consent. Commonly those are most proud who know least; for they do not know themselves. Hence come envy, strife, railings, evil-surmisings, disputes that are all subtlety, and of no solidity, between men of corrupt and carnal minds, ignorant of the truth and its sanctifying power, and seeking their worldly advantage. ( [1Tim.6.6-1Tim.6.10] 1Ti 6:6-10)
[1Tim.6.6-1Tim.6.10]
Verses 6-10
Those that make a trade of Christianity to serve their turn for this world, will be disappointed; but those who mind it as their calling, will find it has the promise of the life that now is, as well as of that which is to come. He that is godly, is sure to be happy in another world; and if contented with his condition in this world, he has enough; and all truly godly people are content. When brought into the greatest straits, we cannot be poorer than when we came into this world; a shroud, a coffin, and a grave, are all that the richest man in the world can have from all his wealth. If nature should be content with a little, grace should be content with less. The necessaries of life bound a true Christian's desires, and with these he will endeavour to be content. We see here the evil of covetousness. It is not said, they that are rich, but they will be rich; who place their happiness in wealth, and are eager and determined in the pursuit. Those that are such, give to Satan the opportunity of tempting them, leading them to use dishonest means, and other bad practices, to add to their gains. Also, leading into so many employments, and such a hurry of business, as leave no time or inclination for spiritual religion; leading to connexions that draw into sin and folly. What sins will not men be drawn into by the love of money! People may have money, and yet not love it; but if they love it, this will push them on to all evil. Every sort of wickedness and vice, in one way or another, grows from the love of money. We cannot look around without perceiving many proofs of this, especially in a day of outward prosperity, great expenses, and loose profession.
[1Tim.6.11-1Tim.6.16]
Verses 11-16
It ill becomes any men, but especially men of God, to set their hearts upon the things of this world; men of God should be taken up with the things of God. There must be a conflict with corruption, and temptations, and the powers of darkness. Eternal life is the crown proposed for our encouragement. We are called to lay hold thereon. To the rich must especially be pointed out their dangers and duties, as to the proper use of wealth. But who can give such a charge, that is not himself above the love of things that wealth can buy? The appearing of Christ is certain, but it is not for us to know the time. Mortal eyes cannot bear the brightness of the Divine glory. None can approach him except as he is made known unto sinners in and by Christ. The Godhead is here adored without distinction of Persons, as all these things are properly spoken, whether of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Ghost. God is revealed to us, only in and through the human nature of Christ, as the only begotten Son of the Father.
[1Tim.6.17-1Tim.6.21]
Verses 17-21
Being rich in this world is wholly different from being rich towards God. Nothing is more uncertain than worldly wealth. Those who are rich, must see that God gives them their riches; and he only can give to enjoy them richly; for many have riches, but enjoy them poorly, not having a heart to use them. What is the best estate worth, more than as it gives opportunity of doing the more good? Showing faith in Christ by fruits of love, let us lay hold on eternal life, when the self-indulgent, covetous, and ungodly around, lift up their eyes in torment. That learning which opposes the truth of the gospel, is not true science, or real knowledge, or it would approve the gospel, and consent to it. Those who advance reason above faith, are in danger of leaving faith. Grace includes all that is good, and grace is an earnest, a beginning of glory; wherever God gives grace, he will give glory.
